modules.description: Practical rituals and presence practices for peak performance when it matters most.

lessons.title: Morning Rituals That Prime You
lessons.content:
## Morning Rituals That Prime You

The hour before an interview is not the time to review your notes one more time. If you don't know it now, you won't learn it in sixty minutes. What you can do is ensure you walk in in the best possible state.

### A Morning Protocol for Interview Days

**1. Don't start with your phone (30 minutes)**
The first inputs of the day shape your nervous system for hours. Notifications, news, and social media create a low-grade reactive state. Protect your morning.

**2. Move your body (15-20 minutes)**
Even a brisk walk changes your chemistry. Movement raises dopamine and norepinephrine — the neurochemicals of focus and motivation. You'll think more clearly and feel more alert.

**3. Review your anchors, not your material**
An anchor is a story, a phrase, or an image that reconnects you with your best self. Choose two or three. *A project you're proud of. A moment you helped someone. A time you surprised yourself.* Revisit these — not to rehearse, but to remember who you are.

**4. Eat something real**
A blood sugar crash mid-interview is a real risk. Eat a light, protein-forward meal two to three hours before.

**5. Arrive early enough to arrive calm**
Build in a thirty-minute buffer beyond what you think you need. Sit somewhere quiet. Take your three breaths. Do one final review of your key stories — not to memorise, but to feel ready.

The goal of the morning is not to become a different person. It's to show up as the best version of the one you already are.

lessons.title: Body Language & First Impressions
lessons.content:
## Body Language & First Impressions

Research from Harvard Business School suggests that interviewers often decide whether they like a candidate within the first thirty seconds. What they're reading in that time is almost entirely non-verbal.

This doesn't mean you need to perform confidence. It means you need to be present in your body — which is something quite different.

### The Elements That Matter

**Posture**
Stand and sit tall — not rigid, but upright. Slouching signals low energy. Excessive rigidity signals anxiety. The sweet spot is grounded and open: chest forward, shoulders back and down, feet planted.

**Eye Contact**
Steady but not intense. In a one-on-one, aim to hold eye contact about sixty percent of the time. In a panel, rotate naturally — giving each person moments of genuine attention.

**The Handshake**
Firm, brief, warm. Match the pressure of the other person. Avoid the limp fish and the bone-crusher equally.

**Hand Gestures**
Natural gestures make you more persuasive and easier to listen to. They indicate engagement. Keeping your hands in your lap signals uncertainty; wild gestures are distracting. Use them freely within the midline of your body.

**What You Do with Silence**
When you need a moment to think, take it. A two-second pause before answering is a sign of thoughtfulness, not incompetence. Nodding while thinking, or saying "that's a great question" to buy time, are tells that undermine confidence.

**The Departure**
How you leave the room matters as much as how you enter it. Thank them genuinely, by name if you know it. The last impression lingers.

lessons.title: Closing Strong — Questions That Impress
lessons.content:
## Closing Strong — Questions That Impress

"Do you have any questions for us?" is not the afterthought it sounds like. It's an opportunity — often the last one — to demonstrate how you think, how seriously you've taken the conversation, and whether you're genuinely curious about the role.

Most candidates ask about salary, hours, or benefits. These are valid questions, but they signal a transactional mindset. The candidates who are remembered ask something different.

### Questions That Signal Real Thinking

**About the role:**
> *"What does success look like at the end of the first six months in this role?"*

This shows you're already thinking about outcomes and accountability — not just getting the job, but doing it well.

**About the team:**
> *"What's the most significant challenge the team is working through right now?"*

This signals that you're a problem-solver looking to contribute, and gives you valuable information about the environment.

**About the culture:**
> *"What do you think people here get wrong about what it takes to succeed?"*

This is a bold question that invites honesty — and often surfaces insights no polished answer would give you.

**Personal to the interviewer:**
> *"What's kept you here?"*

People love talking about why they stayed. The answer tells you more about a company than any recruitment brochure.

### What Not to Ask

Don't ask anything you could have found in the first paragraph of their website. It signals you didn't prepare. And avoid anything that makes it sound like you've already accepted the job before it's offered.

The question you close with is the last impression. Make it count.

swadhyay-the-ancient-word-that-became-my.title: Swadhyay: The Ancient Word That Became My Life's Work
swadhyay-the-ancient-word-that-became-my.excerpt: Swadhyay means 'self-study' in Sanskrit. It's a concept from the Yoga Sutras that has been guiding humans toward self-knowledge for millennia. Here's how it became the foundation of everything I do.
swadhyay-the-ancient-word-that-became-my.content:
# Swadhyay: The Ancient Word That Became My Life's Work

There's a version of this essay where I tell you I always knew I'd spend my life helping people know themselves. But that would be fiction.

The truth is, I came to this work sideways — through confusion of my own, through a period in my early thirties where I had achieved everything I was supposed to want and felt, bewilderingly, like I was disappearing.

It was in that confusion that I first encountered the word Swadhyay.

## The Yoga Sutras

The *Yoga Sutras of Patanjali* is a 2,000-year-old text that most Westerners know only through the physical postures they associate with yoga. But yoga — in its original conception — is a comprehensive system for understanding and transforming human consciousness.

The Sutras outline eight "limbs" of practice, and the second limb — the *niyamas*, or personal observances — includes five qualities to cultivate. The fourth is *Swadhyay*.

Swa means "self." Adhyay means "to study" or "to inquire into." Together: self-study. The ongoing practice of honest self-observation.

Patanjali is specific about what Swadhyay is for: *"Swadhyayat ishta devata samprayogah"* — through self-study, one comes into union with one's true nature.

The word "union" is important. Not improvement. Not achievement. Union — a coming-home to what was always already there.

## What I Understood, Eventually

When I first read this, I thought I understood it. I had been in various kinds of therapy. I had done some meditation. I had journalled for years. Surely this was familiar territory.

It took me a long time to understand the difference between self-analysis and self-study.

Self-analysis is the activity of the thinking mind looking at itself. It is useful — I am not dismissing it. But it has a ceiling, because the instrument doing the examining is also the object being examined. We can only think what we're capable of thinking.

Self-study, in the Swadhyay sense, is something quieter. It is observation without agenda. Curiosity without conclusion. The willingness to look at what's actually here — in the thoughts, in the body, in the patterns — without immediately trying to fix or improve or explain.

It is harder than it sounds. And it leads somewhere that thinking alone cannot reach.

## How It Shapes My Practice

Everything in my coaching work — the one-on-one sessions, the immersion retreats, the courses I've developed — is built around this one concept.

Not self-improvement (though improvement often follows). Not performance enhancement (though performance often improves). But genuine self-knowledge: the kind that changes your relationship with yourself, your decisions, your relationships, and your work.

I have watched this process unfold in hundreds of people. I am still watching it unfold in myself.

What I can say, after twenty-five years, is this: the people who invest in genuine self-knowledge — who take the time to ask and honestly answer the question *Who am I?* — make better decisions, build better relationships, lead more effectively, and live with greater ease.

Not because life becomes simpler. It doesn't. But because they meet it from a more stable, more honest, more fully themselves place.

## The Invitation

Swadhyay is not a destination. It is a practice — one that unfolds over a lifetime, deepening rather than finishing.

Every course I teach, every retreat I facilitate, every coaching conversation I hold is, in some form, an invitation into this practice.

Not to find the final answer to who you are — there isn't one. But to begin, or deepen, the inquiry. To take the question seriously. To trust that the looking itself has value.

*That is Swadhyay. And that is the work.*
swadhyay-the-ancient-word-that-became-my.author: Neha Sharma

leadership-presence-is-not-what-you-thin.title: Leadership Presence Is Not What You Think
leadership-presence-is-not-what-you-thin.excerpt: Most people think presence is about being loud, forceful, or commanding. In 25 years of executive coaching, I've found the opposite is true.
leadership-presence-is-not-what-you-thin.content:
# Leadership Presence Is Not What You Think

When I ask leaders to describe someone who has genuine executive presence, they almost always use words like: commanding, powerful, confident, magnetic.

And then I ask them to think about the most present leader they've ever actually worked with — not the most impressive-sounding one, but the one whose presence they actually felt in the room. And they pause. And the words they use become quite different.

*Calm. Attentive. Honest. Real.*

This gap — between what we think presence looks like and what it actually feels like — is at the heart of why so many leadership development programmes miss the mark.

## The Performance Problem

The kind of presence that gets taught in most training programmes is a performance. Stand here. Speak at this pace. Project from the diaphragm. Command the room.

These techniques are not without value. But they address the outside without touching the inside. And the result is leaders who seem confident but don't feel trustworthy — who project authority but don't create psychological safety — who are impressive to be around but exhausting to work for.

The performance of presence is recognisable. And it is fundamentally limited, because it is, at its core, a form of control. And people can sense when they're being managed rather than met.

## What Genuine Presence Actually Is

In my experience, genuine presence has one essential quality: **full attention**.

When a leader is fully present — not planning their next comment while you speak, not subtly checking their phone, not elsewhere in their mind — you feel it. There is something unusually settling about being truly seen and heard.

This is not charisma. It is not performance. It is the simple, rare, and profoundly powerful act of giving another person your complete attention.

The paradox is that this makes you more compelling, not less. We are drawn to people who are fully present because it is so unusual — and because it meets a deep human need.

## What Gets in the Way

If genuine presence is simply full attention, why is it so rare?

Because full attention is difficult. Our nervous systems are wired for threat detection, not presence. We are constantly scanning — for how we're being perceived, for what comes next, for potential problems.

Add to this the relentless pace of modern leadership — back-to-back meetings, always-on communication, the sense that everything is urgent — and the conditions for presence are almost never met.

Developing genuine presence requires swimming against this current. It requires the willingness to slow down when everything says to speed up, to listen when the temptation is to speak, to be uncertain rather than performing confidence.

It is, in the end, a practice of courage — the courage to stop managing impressions and simply show up as you are.

## Three Practices That Develop Real Presence

**1. The minute before**
Before any significant interaction — a meeting, a conversation, a presentation — take sixty seconds to arrive. Breathe. Feel the ground under your feet. Set an intention for who you want to be in this exchange, not what you want to get from it.

**2. Put your phone away (actually away)**
Not face-down. Not in your pocket. Out of sight. The visible phone is a signal to everyone in the room that you might leave at any moment. Its absence is the signal that you're staying.

**3. Listen to understand, not to respond**
In your next one-on-one, try this: don't plan your response while the other person is speaking. Just listen. Notice what they're saying beyond the words. Notice what they're not saying. Then take a breath before you reply.

This is harder than it sounds. And its effect on the person you're with is immediate.

---

*Presence is not a management skill. It is a human quality — one that can be developed, but only if we're willing to examine what's actually getting in the way.*

the-interview-mindset-shift-that-gets-pe.excerpt: The most common interview mistake I see? Treating it like a test. It's not. It's a conversation. Here's what shifts when you make that one change.
the-interview-mindset-shift-that-gets-pe.content:
# The Interview Mindset Shift That Gets People Hired

I've helped a lot of people prepare for interviews. And across all the different coaching, all the practice questions, all the feedback on how to structure a story — there is usually one shift that matters more than all of the others combined.

It is this: **stop treating the interview like a test.**

## The Test Mindset

When we walk into an interview thinking it's a test, everything changes — and not for the better.

We become focused on giving the "right" answers rather than the honest ones. We start performing rather than communicating. We read every facial expression for evidence of how we're doing. We become so focused on impressing that we stop listening.

The test mindset also creates a particular kind of anxiety — the anxiety of not knowing whether you've passed or failed, with no way to know until it's over. This anxiety is counterproductive in an obvious way: the more anxious you are, the worse you perform; the worse you perform, the more anxious you become.

## The Conversation Mindset

Now imagine walking into that same room thinking: *this is a conversation between two professionals exploring whether there's a genuine fit.*

Not a one-way evaluation. A mutual exploration.

Something shifts. You become curious about the person across from you — what are they like, what matters to them, what problems are they actually trying to solve? You start listening more carefully, because what they say matters to you too. You ask better questions, because you genuinely want to know the answers.

And — crucially — when you speak about your experience, you speak more naturally, because you're not performing. You're sharing.

## The Practical Difference

Here's what this looks like in practice:

**In a test mindset:** When asked "What's your greatest weakness?", you deliver the pre-prepared answer about how you sometimes work too hard or care too much.

**In a conversation mindset:** You answer genuinely. You name something real you've struggled with, what you've learned from it, and where you are now. You trust that honesty is more compelling than performance — because it is.

**In a test mindset:** When you get an unexpected question, you panic.

**In a conversation mindset:** When you get an unexpected question, you're curious. You take a breath, think for a moment, and say what's actually true.

## The Double Shift

The mindset shift also has a second dimension, beyond just what happens inside you.

When you treat the interview as a conversation, you also become genuinely curious about whether *you* want this job, this company, this manager. You evaluate as well as being evaluated.

This changes the power dynamic — not in an aggressive or manipulative way, but in the most accurate way. The interview is genuinely mutual. Two parties figuring out whether something is right for both of them.

Clients who make this shift report that they perform better — but also that they leave interviews knowing more clearly whether they actually want the role.

That's the full value of the shift: better performance *and* better decisions.

---

*If you're preparing for an interview soon, try this: before you walk in, remind yourself that you're also interviewing them. Let genuine curiosity about them be part of your preparation — not just rehearsal of your answers.*

*Notice what changes.*

what-25-years-of-coaching-taught-me-abou.title: What 25 Years of Coaching Taught Me About Fear
what-25-years-of-coaching-taught-me-abou.excerpt: Fear is not the enemy. It's a messenger. The question is — are you listening?
what-25-years-of-coaching-taught-me-abou.content:
# What 25 Years of Coaching Taught Me About Fear

I have sat with a lot of fear.

In twenty-five years of coaching, across hundreds of clients — leaders, founders, young professionals, people at the edge of major life transitions — there is one thing that shows up in almost every session, regardless of the presenting problem.

Fear. In one form or another.

And what I've learned about it — slowly, imperfectly, through many mistakes — is this: the way most of us have been taught to relate to fear is exactly backwards.

## Fear as Enemy

The dominant cultural story about fear is that it's an obstacle. Something to be overcome, pushed through, or conquered. "Feel the fear and do it anyway." "Courage is doing it even when you're afraid."

There's something right about this. Action in the face of fear is often necessary and admirable.

But there's something missing too. If we treat fear purely as an obstacle, we miss what it's telling us — and we lose access to some of the most important information we have.

## Fear as Messenger

Every client who has ever sat in front of me feeling afraid about something significant is being told something by that fear. Not necessarily the thing they think they're being told — fear often speaks in distortion, especially when it's long-standing — but something real.

The senior leader afraid to give his team more autonomy is often afraid of becoming unnecessary. That's worth knowing.

The young professional terrified of leaving a stable job is often carrying a belief that she doesn't have what it takes without the structure. That's worth examining.

The founder who can't delegate is often afraid that if others do the work, he won't be seen as the creator. That, too, is information.

Fear is a messenger. And like any messenger, it's worth asking: what exactly are you trying to tell me?

## Three Questions I Ask About Fear

When a client is in the grip of significant fear, I don't move immediately to action. I move to curiosity.

**"What exactly are you afraid of?"**
Not the surface answer. The specific, honest one. "I'm afraid of failing" is a start; "I'm afraid that if this doesn't work, it will prove that I was right not to trust myself" is the real one.

**"What would you do if you knew you couldn't fail?"**
Not as a motivational exercise — as a diagnostic one. The answer often reveals what someone actually wants, unclouded by the fear of failure. That clarity is sometimes more useful than the action itself.

**"What is this fear protecting you from?"**
Fear is, at its root, protective. Even the fears that hold us back were once (or still are) protecting something valuable. Identifying what a fear is protecting often creates compassion for it — and compassion is usually more effective than confrontation.

## What Fear Is Not

Fear is not a verdict on your worth, your competence, or your future. It is not a sign that you should stop. And it is not the enemy.

It is part of you — the part that cares deeply about something and is worried about losing it.

When I've seen clients genuinely shift their relationship with fear — not eliminate it, but stop fighting it — something remarkable happens. The energy that was going into suppression or avoidance becomes available for the thing they actually care about.

*That* is when things begin to change.

the-hidden-cost-of-not-knowing-your-valu.title: The Hidden Cost of Not Knowing Your Values
the-hidden-cost-of-not-knowing-your-valu.excerpt: Every time you say yes to something that violates your values, you lose a little bit of yourself. The cost is invisible — until it isn't.
the-hidden-cost-of-not-knowing-your-valu.content:
# The Hidden Cost of Not Knowing Your Values

I have a client — I'll call her Priya — who spent eight years at a company she didn't believe in. She was very good at her job. She received excellent performance reviews. She was promoted twice. She made good money.

She also, for eight years, felt a low-grade wrongness she couldn't name.

When we finally got to the root of it, the diagnosis was simple: every major decision the company made violated one of her core values. She valued transparency; the company rewarded opacity. She valued collaborative decision-making; the culture was hierarchical and top-down. She valued integrity over short-term results; the pressure was always for quarterly numbers.

She knew none of this consciously. She had never articulated her values, even to herself. She just knew something was wrong — and spent eight years trying to make peace with it.

## What Values Actually Are

Values are not aspirations. They are not the qualities you wish you had, or think you should have, or present to the world as your own. They are what you actually, demonstrably, care most about — revealed not in what you say, but in what you do when it costs you something.

If honesty is a value but you regularly tell small lies to avoid discomfort, honesty is not currently one of your operating values. That's not a judgement — it's data.

The values that shape your behaviour under pressure, under temptation, under genuine difficulty — those are your real values. And they're worth knowing.

## The Invisible Erosion

When you repeatedly act against your values, something happens that's hard to notice in the moment: you lose credibility with yourself.

Not in a dramatic, crisis-of-faith way. In a quiet, cumulative way. Each small compromise registers somewhere. Each time you say yes to something that feels wrong, the signal that something is wrong becomes a little easier to ignore.

Over time, people in this pattern become detached from their own instincts. They have trouble making decisions. They don't trust their own judgement. They've learned, through practice, to override the part of themselves that knows.

This is the hidden cost of not knowing your values: not just bad choices, but the gradual erosion of the capacity to know what's right for you.

## How to Start

Values clarification doesn't require a weekend retreat or a life coach (though both can help). It requires honesty and a little time.

Start here:

**Think of three decisions you've made that you're genuinely proud of.** Not because they worked out — but because they felt right, even when they were hard. What value was being expressed in each one?

**Think of three situations that made you genuinely angry.** Not annoyed — angry. Anger is almost always a values violation. What value was being stepped on?

**Think of what you'd refuse to do for money.** The things we won't trade away are usually the things we care about most.

From these three exercises, a pattern will emerge. That pattern is your values.

---

*Priya left the company. She took a role that paid less and had a smaller title. Six months later, she told me it was the best professional decision she'd ever made. Not because everything is easy — it isn't — but because she no longer carries the low-grade wrongness.*

*Knowing your values doesn't guarantee you'll always act on them. But you can't act on what you can't name.*
the-hidden-cost-of-not-knowing-your-valu.author: Neha Sharma

eft-tapping-calm-anxious-mind.title: How EFT Tapping Calmed My Most Anxious Clients
eft-tapping-calm-anxious-mind.excerpt: Three minutes. That's often all it takes. Here's exactly what I do with clients who walk in with hearts pounding and minds racing.
eft-tapping-calm-anxious-mind.content:
# How EFT Tapping Calmed My Most Anxious Clients

I still remember the first time I used EFT with a client. She was a senior executive preparing for a board presentation — the most important of her career. She arrived at our session unable to complete a sentence. Her hands were shaking. She had barely slept.

We had forty-five minutes. I had two choices: talk through the anxiety, which I knew from experience would help only moderately, or try something I'd recently trained in but not yet used in practice.

I chose EFT.

Twenty minutes later, she was laughing. Not the hollow, nervous laughter of someone pretending to be fine — but genuine amusement at how different she felt. "I feel like someone turned the volume down," she said. "Everything is still real — the stakes, the pressure — but it's not inside me the same way."

She gave the best presentation of her career.

## What I Actually Do

When a client arrives in acute anxiety, I don't immediately go to content. The thinking mind is offline when the nervous system is in threat response — no amount of reframing will land.

I start with the body.

**Step 1: Name and rate it**
"On a scale of 0 to 10, where is this right now?" The act of rating — of observing the emotion with enough distance to assign it a number — already creates a small but crucial shift from being inside the emotion to looking at it.

**Step 2: The setup statement**
We tap on the side of the hand (the karate chop point) while saying:

*"Even though I feel this intense anxiety in my chest — and my mind won't stop racing — I deeply and completely accept myself."*

The statement does something paradoxical: it acknowledges the problem fully while also introducing self-acceptance. Most anxious people are not only anxious — they're anxious about being anxious. The setup statement begins to break that cycle.

**Step 3: Tapping through the points**
We move through the standard sequence — eyebrow, side of eye, under eye, under nose, chin, collarbone, underarm, top of head — while speaking the feeling honestly:

*"This anxiety... this racing heart... what if I fail... what if they can see it... I can't calm down..."*

**Step 4: Re-rate**
After one round — which takes about two to three minutes — we check the number. In my experience, it almost always drops. Often significantly.

## The Question I'm Always Asked

"Does this really work, or is it placebo?"

Honest answer: probably some of both, and I'm not sure it matters.

What I know is this: cortisol levels in people who tap are measurably lower than in control groups after sessions. Multiple randomised controlled trials support EFT's effectiveness for anxiety and PTSD. And I have sat with hundreds of people in states of genuine distress and watched something shift in their bodies and faces that no amount of talking alone produced.

The mechanism is still being studied. The effect is consistent.

## A Simple Sequence You Can Try Today

If you're experiencing anxiety right now — or want something to use the next time it arrives — here is the basic sequence:

1. Rate your anxiety (0-10)
2. Tap the side of your hand and say: *"Even though I feel this anxiety, I accept myself."* (x3)
3. Tap through eyebrow, side of eye, under eye, under nose, chin, collarbone, underarm, top of head, saying: *"This anxiety... this feeling in my body... it's real... I'm tapping anyway..."*
4. Take a breath. Re-rate.
5. If still above 3, repeat. If below 3, try a positive round: *"I am calming... I can handle this... I am safe..."*

Most people notice a shift within a single round. The first time you feel it — that unexpected dropping of intensity — it tends to be memorable.

why-emotional-intelligence-is-the-new-le.excerpt: The leaders who last aren't the smartest ones in the room. They're the ones who know themselves well enough to manage what happens inside them when the pressure is on.
why-emotional-intelligence-is-the-new-le.content:
# Why Emotional Intelligence Is the New Leadership IQ

In 1995, Daniel Goleman published a book that changed how organisations think about leadership. *Emotional Intelligence* argued that IQ — long the gold standard of professional competence — explained less than 20% of the variance in professional success. The rest was something else.

Goleman called it EQ: the ability to recognise, understand, and manage emotions — both your own and others'.

Thirty years later, the research has only become more robust. And in my own work with leaders across industries and seniority levels, the pattern is consistent: the leaders who create lasting impact are not the most technically brilliant. They are the most emotionally intelligent.

## What EQ Actually Is

Emotional intelligence is often misunderstood as "being nice" or "being sensitive." It is neither.

EQ, in its most rigorous form, consists of four domains:

**Self-awareness** — the capacity to accurately perceive your own emotions and how they influence your thinking and behaviour.

**Self-management** — the ability to regulate your emotions under pressure — not suppress them, but channel them constructively.

**Social awareness** — the capacity to accurately read others: their emotions, their motivations, their unspoken concerns.

**Relationship management** — the ability to use emotional insight to guide interactions, navigate conflict, and inspire people toward shared goals.

The leaders I've worked with who excel across all four domains are, without exception, the ones their teams would follow into genuine difficulty — not out of obligation, but out of genuine trust.

## The High-IQ Trap

Here is the cruel irony of high cognitive intelligence in leadership: the very qualities that create analytical brilliance can work against emotional intelligence.

The pattern I see most often: a highly intelligent leader who has spent twenty years being rewarded for being the smartest person in the room. They're quick, decisive, and confident. They solve problems before others have finished defining them.

And then they wonder why their team doesn't bring them problems early. Why the best people leave. Why meetings feel like performances rather than genuine conversations.

The intelligence that got them there is not the intelligence required to lead well.

## Three Habits That Build EQ

EQ is not fixed. It is a set of skills, and like all skills, it can be developed.

**1. Name your emotions with precision**
Most people have a vocabulary of about three emotional states: good, bad, and stressed. Research shows that "emotional granularity" — the ability to precisely name what you're feeling — significantly improves your ability to regulate those feelings. There is a meaningful difference between "anxious" and "overwhelmed," between "frustrated" and "disappointed."

Practice: At the end of each day, name three emotions you experienced and what triggered each.

**2. Pause before you respond**
The space between stimulus and response is where EQ lives. Under pressure, most of us collapse that space — we react before we've chosen our response. The discipline of the pause — even a breath, even three seconds — is the most immediate and impactful EQ practice I know.

**3. Get curious about what others are feeling**
Not as manipulation, but as genuine interest. Before your next difficult conversation, ask yourself: "What is this person most afraid of? What do they most need from this exchange?" Answering those questions honestly changes everything about how you show up.

---

*None of this is soft. Leading with emotional intelligence is one of the most demanding — and most rewarding — things a leader can develop. It requires the kind of honesty that most of us find genuinely difficult.*

*But the leaders who do this work create something rare: organisations where people bring their whole selves, take genuine risks, and stay.*
why-emotional-intelligence-is-the-new-le.author: Neha Sharma

the-question-that-changes-everything.title: The Question That Changes Everything
the-question-that-changes-everything.excerpt: For 25 years I've been asking my clients one question. It's the same question that stopped me in my tracks at 32. And it's the reason I named my practice Swadhyay.
the-question-that-changes-everything.content:
# The Question That Changes Everything

I was thirty-two years old, sitting in a coaching session I hadn't asked for — it was offered by my company as part of a leadership development programme — when the coach asked me a question I'd never been asked before.

Not "Where do you want to be in five years?" Not "What are your strengths?" Not even "What's holding you back?"

She asked: **"Who are you?"**

Not "What do you do." Not "What have you achieved." Not "How are you perceived." But: who, underneath all of that, are you?

I sat in silence for a long time. And in that silence, I realised I had absolutely no idea.

## What Swadhyay Means

*Swadhyay* is a Sanskrit word from the ancient Indian philosophical tradition. It translates, most directly, as "self-study" — though that translation doesn't quite capture the weight of it.

In the Yoga Sutras of Patanjali, one of the oldest and most comprehensive texts on human consciousness, Swadhyay is listed as one of the *niyamas* — the personal observances that form the foundation of a conscious life. It sits alongside *tapas* (discipline) and *ishvara pranidhana* (surrender to something larger than yourself).

The placement is deliberate. Self-study comes before almost everything else — because without genuine self-knowledge, all other effort operates in the dark.

## The Paradox

Here is what strikes me after twenty-five years of working with people: the more successful someone is, the less time they've usually spent on this question.

The early years of a career reward performance, not reflection. You're evaluated on what you deliver, not on who you are. And so most people learn to focus outward — on results, on reputation, on the next goal — and inward attention becomes a luxury for later.

Later rarely comes.

The senior leader who suddenly, at fifty, feels empty despite every external marker of success. The professional who can't explain why a dream job feels wrong. The parent who has given everything to their children and doesn't know who they are apart from that role.

This isn't failure. It's a very human pattern. And it has a very human solution: the willingness to ask the question — and to sit with the not-knowing long enough for something true to emerge.

## What the Question Does

I don't give my clients the answer. I can't — I don't have it. What I do is create the conditions in which they can begin to find their own.

What I've observed, over and over, is this: something shifts when people genuinely begin to ask. Not answer — ask. The quality of their decisions changes. The relationships they invest in change. Their relationship with fear changes.

They begin, as one client put it, to live from the inside out rather than the outside in.

That is what Swadhyay, at its best, makes possible. Not a final answer to who you are — the inquiry is ongoing, as it should be. But a genuine acquaintance with yourself that changes everything that follows.

---

*If this resonates with you, I'd encourage you to spend just five minutes with the question today. Not to answer it — just to sit with it. Notice what comes up. That noticing is the beginning.*
